sections.title: Reading Comprehension · Passage B
sections.intro: Read the poem “Machines” and answer questions 11–14. Vocabulary notes follow the poem.

passage.title: Machines
passage.credit: —Daniel Whitehead Hicky · from Bright Harbor, 1932 · Henry Holt and Company

lines.text: I hear them grinding, grinding, through the night,
The gaunt machines with arteries of fire,
Muscled with iron, boweled with smoldering light;
I watch them pulsing, swinging, climbing higher,
Derrick¹ on derrick, wheel on rhythmic wheel,
Swift band on whirring band, lever on lever,
Shouting their songs in raucous notes of steel,
Blinding a village with light, damming a river.
I hear them grinding, grinding, hour on hour,
Cleaving the night in twain,² shattering the dark
With all the rasping torrents of their power,
Groaning and belching spark on crimson spark.
I cannot hear my voice above their cry
Shaking the earth and thundering to the sky.
Slowly the dawn comes up. No motors stir
The brightening hilltops as the sunrise flows
In yellow tides where daybreak’s lavender
Clings to a waiting valley. No derrick throws
The sun into the heavens and no pulley
Unfolds the wildflowers thirsting for the day;
No wheel unravels ferns deep in a gulley;
No engine starts the brook upon its way.
The butterflies drift idly, wing to wing,
Knowing no measured rhythm they must follow;
No turbine drives the white clouds as they swing
Across the cool blue meadows of the swallow.
With all the feathered silence of a swan
They whirr and beat—the engines of the dawn.
¹ derrick — a large machine used for lifting
² twain — two

questions.prompt: The figurative language in lines 2 and 3 contributes to the poem’s meaning by

choices.text: expressing a frustration with the loss of nature
establishing a parallel between man and machine
affirming the essential human need for machines
illustrating the struggle for society’s survival

questions.explanation: Calling machines “gaunt,” giving them “arteries,” and describing them as “muscled” likens their parts to a human body. This establishes a parallel between people and machines.

questions.prompt: The description of the machines’ songs as “raucous” (line 7) conveys that the songs are
questions.explanation: The machines grind, rasp, groan, and drown out the speaker’s voice. “Raucous” adds to that picture of loud, harsh noise.

questions.prompt: The poet’s use of “groaning and belching” (line 12) is used to convey
questions.explanation: The strained bodily sounds make the machines seem to labor as they throw sparks and grind through the night. They convey effort and difficult work, not affection.

questions.prompt: A central idea reinforced by lines 27 and 28 is that nature
questions.explanation: The dawn’s “engines” work with the “feathered silence of a swan,” contrasting with the noisy, laboring factory machines. Nature brings about morning smoothly and quietly.
